title: Experiences and acceptability of group‐based, remotely delivered functional imagery training intervention for weight loss: A qualitative study
abstract: Abstract Objectives Many weight management interventions prioritize education and behavioural prescription over the motivational processes that sustain change. Functional Imagery Training (FIT), a motivational intervention that uses multisensory imagery, has supported weight loss when delivered individually. This study explored participants' views of FIT and the acceptability of delivering it remotely to small groups. Design Qualitative interview study embedded in a single‐arm feasibility study and the intervention arm of a pilot randomized controlled trial of remotely delivered FIT for adults with a body mass index (BMI) over 35 kg/m 2 . Methods Participants attended four FIT sessions delivered by video conference in small groups over 6 weeks. Thirty‐two participants (28 female; aged 25–71 years) completed one‐to‐one semi‐structured interviews approximately 6 weeks post‐intervention. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results Of five themes, three addressed participants' views of FIT: FIT as a practical bridge between knowing and doing; imagery as a tool for regulating emotional eating; and FIT as a non‐judgemental alternative to healthcare encounters experienced as stigmatizing. Two addressed the acceptability of delivery: remote delivery as accessible and psychologically safe; and peer support as normalizing and motivating. Some participants wanted longer or more frequent sessions. Conclusions Among participants who engaged, group‐based, remotely delivered FIT was described as acceptable and personally meaningful. Interviewees lost more weight than the wider sample, and almost half of those randomized to FIT in the pilot trial did not attend a session, so these views may not reflect those of non‐attenders. Psychologically stigma‐sensitive and flexible delivery, group‐based, remotely delivered FIT was experienced as acceptable and psychologically meaningful. The findings highlight the importance of psychologically informed, stigma‐sensitive and flexible delivery; warrants further evaluation models in supporting engagement with weight management interventions.
